477.title: Living ashtpadi 10
477.hook: seeing the countless makes our worries smaller
477.tomorrow: Ashtpadi 11, salok: the doer of all
477.howItsDone: Sikhs read the 'kaee kot' stanzas of Sukhmani Sahib, and Japji's lines on countless worlds, as hymns of wonder that put personal troubles in the setting of a vast creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kartaa: the proud and the lost, counted too, and only the Creator knows them. Your line was all in the play. Today, ashtpadi ten, lived.

It's two in the morning, and a worry has taken over the whole room. An email you shouldn't have sent. A bill. A test result. Lying in bed, it feels like the biggest thing in the universe. Then you get up for water, glance out the window, and there, if the sky is clear, are the stars. More than you can count, and more behind those. The worry doesn't vanish. But it shrinks, a little, to its real size. Astronomers didn't invent that feeling, and neither did poets. Ashtpadi ten knew it too.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING, ONE WORRY.` → `A GLANCE AT THE STARS.` → `THE WORRY FINDS ITS REAL SIZE.`

segments.voice: After counting the seekers and the lost, ashtpadi ten widens further. Its drumbeat, kaee kot, many millions, moves from people to worlds. One stanza says: many millions are the sources of life and the regions of the earth. Many millions are the skies and the brahmands. Brahmand is a universe, a whole world-system. Many millions of universes. Guru Nanak said something similar in Japji, which we read last year: worlds below worlds, hundreds of thousands of skies above skies, and people grow tired searching for the limit. The Granth isn't giving an astronomy lesson here. It's giving a sense of scale: vast, uncountable, beyond any edge anyone can find. So what does living this mean? Put simply: seeing the countless makes our worries smaller. Not unimportant. Smaller. Your worry is real, and it's yours, and in Sukhmani's picture the Creator of many millions of universes holds it too. But it's not the center of everything. That's the gift of ashtpadi ten. It takes you outside on a clear night and says: look how big this is, look how much is being held, and see what size your worry really is.
screen: `FROM PEOPLE TO WORLDS.` · `BRAHMAND: A WHOLE UNIVERSE.` · `JAPJI: SKIES ABOVE SKIES.` · `NOT UNIMPORTANT, JUST SMALLER.` · then, large: `SMALLER WORRIES.`

segments.voice: If it's night, step outside or go to a window; if it's day, close your eyes and picture the darkest, clearest sky you've ever seen, and let your eyes go from one star to the next, knowing there are more behind each one. Let one worry come into your mind, place it under that sky, and notice its size now. If you pray, you can hand it over to the One who holds the many millions.
Brahmand, a universe, a whole world-system. Many millions of brahmands and skies: seeing the countless gives our worries back their real size.
Your line: smaller worries. Real, and held, but not the center of everything. Sleep well.

478.title: Ashtpadi 11, salok: the doer of all
478.hook: karan kaaran prabh ek hai: He alone is the doer and the cause
478.howItsDone: Sikhs read this salok at the opening of Sukhmani's eleventh ashtpadi, and teachers draw on 'karan kaaran' to describe working wholeheartedly while trusting the outcome to Waheguru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, brahmand: the stars at two in the morning, and a worry finding its real size. Your line was smaller worries. Today, ashtpadi eleven opens, and names who's behind all those skies.

Watch a toddler with a toy steering wheel in the back seat of a car. He turns it hard left; the car happens to turn left. He shouts with delight. He's sure he did that. He turns it right; the car goes straight. He turns harder. Still straight. Frustration. The grown-ups laugh, because they can see who's actually driving. Then they go back to gripping wheels of their own: the plan, the career, the children's futures, sure that every turn of the road is theirs. The eleventh salok is a short, gentle word about the real driver.
screen: `A TODDLER'S TOY STEERING WHEEL.` → `SURE HE TURNED THE CAR.` → `WHO'S ACTUALLY DRIVING?`

segments.voice: The salok has two lines. The first: karan kaaran prabh ek hai, doosar naahee koe. God alone is the doer and the cause of causes; there is no other. Karan is doing, the deed. Kaaran is the cause, the reason behind the deed. Karan kaaran: the one who does, and the cause behind every cause. Doosar naahee koe: there's no second. The second line: Nanak is a sacrifice to Him, who is in the water, on the land, and in the sky. Balihaar is the word for giving oneself up in love, being a sacrifice to someone. So a line that could sound like cold philosophy, one cause of everything, ends in love, and in a God found everywhere. Now, a careful point. Sikh teaching doesn't say our choices don't matter. Japji says plainly that we ourselves sow and we ourselves eat what we sow. Sikhs are asked to work hard, earn honestly and act. What the salok takes away is not the effort. It's the illusion that we're the only ones driving. You can turn your wheel with all your heart; you just stop believing the whole road answers to you. That's the peace the salok points to: doing your part fully, and leaving the outcome with the doer of all.
screen: `KARAN: THE DOING. KAARAN: THE CAUSE.` · `DOOSAR NAAHEE KOE: NO SECOND.` · `IN WATER, LAND AND SKY.` · `YOUR PART, NOT THE WHOLE ROAD.` · then, large: `HE IS THE DOER.`

segments.voice: Think of an outcome you're gripping right now, an interview, a diagnosis, a child's choice, and honestly name your part in it and whether you've done it. Then picture your hands on that toy steering wheel, feel how tight they are, and loosen them, finger by finger, on the out-breath; you're still in the car, and you still care where it goes. If you pray, you can place the outcome with the doer of all.
Karan kaaran, the doer and the cause of causes. The salok says God alone is this, found in water, land and sky.
Your line: he is the doer. Your part, done fully, and the road left to him. Day four hundred seventy-eight, done.

479.title: His play
479.hook: all happens within His will and His play
479.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of 'bhaana mannana', accepting God's will, especially in grief or hardship, while still working to change what can be changed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karan kaaran, the doer and the cause of causes; your line was he is the doer. Today, the first stanza of ashtpadi eleven.

Rain on the morning of the wedding. A flight canceled. The diagnosis nobody wanted. A baby who arrives three weeks early, on the one day everyone was away. Every life has moments when the plan simply doesn't happen, and nothing you could have done would have changed it. Some people rage. Some go numb. In a Sikh home, an elder may say a short phrase, quietly, sometimes through tears: bhaana mannana. Accept the will. It isn't giving up. It's something harder.
screen: `RAIN ON THE WEDDING DAY.` → `NOTHING YOU COULD HAVE DONE.` → `BHAANA MANNANA: ACCEPT THE WILL.`

segments.voice: The stanza begins: God is able to do, and to have things done. Then: jo tis bhaavai soee hog. Whatever pleases Him comes to pass. Bhaavai and bhaana are one family of words: what pleases God, and so, the will. Then the pictures come fast. In an instant He sets up and takes down. By His order He holds the earth up with no support beneath it. By His order things are born, and by His order they merge back. High and low, every shade and form. He makes and makes, and beholds His own greatness; Nanak, He is pervading all. You might picture a stern ruler issuing commands. But later in Sukhmani, Guru Arjan uses a gentler word for the whole show: khel, play. God makes His own play, the hymn says, and watches it. Picture a child building a sandcastle, delighting in it, letting the tide take it, and building again. Put the will and the play together and you reach the heart of bhaana mannana. For Sikhs, accepting the will isn't accepting that someone up there is cruel. It's trusting that even the rain on the wedding day is inside the play, though no one can see the whole stage. And Sikhs who accept the bhaana still grieve, still fight injustice, still call the doctor. Acceptance is for what you can't change.

segments.voice: Find one thing that's truly fixed, not something you can still work on: the weather, a past event, someone else's choice, a loss. Notice where you push against it in your body, the jaw, the stomach, the shoulders, and breathe into that place; you don't have to like it, only let it be what it is, inside the play. If you pray, you can say the two words Sikhs use: bhaana mannana.
His play. Jo tis bhaavai soee hog: whatever pleases Him comes to pass, and the whole creation is His play, made and watched by its Maker.
Your line: his will. Not giving up, but trusting the play, even on a rainy day. See you tomorrow.

480.title: Nothing outside
480.howItsDone: Sikhs understand hukam, the divine order, as encompassing everything, as Japji puts it, and many recall it in frustration or hardship as a way of loosening the ego's demand that things go its way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, His play: whatever pleases Him comes to pass, and bhaana mannana, accepting the will. Today, the one word that stanza keeps repeating.

You're stuck in traffic. Not moving. You're going to be late, and there's nothing you can do. The jaw sets, the fingers drum, and a voice in your head starts narrating how unfair this is, as if the traffic were happening outside the world, a glitch in how things are supposed to go. Most frustration has that shape: this shouldn't be happening. The first stanza of ashtpadi eleven has a single word it repeats, line after line, that answers the feeling. The word is hukam.
screen: `STUCK IN TRAFFIC.` → `THIS SHOULDN'T BE HAPPENING.` → `ONE WORD, LINE AFTER LINE.`

segments.voice: Hukam is the divine order, the command, the way God's will runs through everything. You met it last year in Japji. Yesterday's pictures, the earth held up with no support, things born and merging back, high and low, every color and form, all ride on one word, opening line after line: hukme, by the order. Guru Nanak said it plainly in Japji: everyone is within the hukam; no one is outside the hukam. Now the traffic jam. Frustration says: this is outside how things should be. Hukam says: there is no outside. The jam is inside the order. So is the meeting you'll be late for. So is your frustration. That doesn't make it pleasant. And it doesn't mean God personally put a truck in your lane to teach you a lesson; Sikh teachers don't usually read hukam as that kind of puzzle. It means the frustrating thing isn't a glitch in the universe. It's part of the same order that holds the earth up. When nothing is outside, there's nothing left to fight the way frustration wants to fight. Japji also says that whoever understands the hukam stops saying I, I, I. The ego is the part that insists things go its way. Nothing outside quietly loosens it.

segments.voice: Bring up something small that annoyed you today, a slow line, a rude message, a broken thing, and feel where it lives in you. Breathing in, say silently: this too is inside; breathing out: nothing outside; and let the feeling stay, held in the same order as everything else, until its edge softens even a little. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on the out-breath.
Nothing outside. Everything is within the hukam, the divine order, even what frustrates us; no one and nothing is outside it.
Your line: this too is inside. Even the traffic, even the frustration. Day four hundred eighty, done.

481.title: Living ashtpadi 11
481.hook: trust and effort together: act, and leave the rest
481.howItsDone: Sikhs hold kirat karni, honest effort and work, together with accepting God's will, and teachers quote Guru Arjan's couplet on udam, effort, as the balance between the two.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nothing outside: the hukam holds everything, even the traffic jam and the frustration. Today, ashtpadi eleven comes off the page and into a working day.

Punjab is farming country, and a farmer there knows something in his bones that the rest of us learn slowly. You plow. You choose good seed and sow it at the right time, straight and deep. You watch the canal, pull the weeds, get up before dawn for months. And then you wait for rain you cannot make, sun you cannot order, and a harvest never entirely yours to decide. A lazy farmer has nothing to harvest. A farmer who thinks he controls the sky wears himself out. The good farmer does both: works, and lets go.
screen: `PLOW, SEED, SOW, WEED.` → `RAIN YOU CANNOT MAKE.` → `WORK, AND LET GO.`

segments.voice: For three days ashtpadi eleven has said God is the doer of all. Karan kaaran, the cause of causes. Jo tis bhaavai soee hog, whatever pleases Him comes to pass. Nothing outside the hukam. Heard alone, that could sound like a reason to sit on the porch. Sikh teaching doesn't read it that way. Guru Arjan, who wrote Sukhmani, wrote a couplet elsewhere in the Guru Granth Sahib: make the effort, and live; earn, and enjoy peace; meditate, and meet God; Nanak, then anxiety is gone. The word for effort is udam: striving, enterprise, getting up and doing. So the Sikh picture has two hands. One works: udam, honest labor, what Sikhs call kirat karni, earning by your own effort. The other opens: bhaana, trust, leaving the outcome to the doer of all. Neither hand alone is the path. Effort without trust becomes anxiety, gripping the wheel of the whole road. Trust without effort becomes an excuse. Together they give what the couplet promises: anxiety is gone. Not because everything works out, but because you did your part fully and stopped carrying the part that was never yours. Like the farmer: plow as if it all depends on you, then look at the sky as if it all depends on God.

segments.voice: Picture one task in front of you today and see yourself doing it fully, hands busy, giving it real effort. Then picture it done, the email sent, the meal served, and open your hands, palms up, like a farmer looking at the sky. Breathe in: I act; breathe out: I release; and if you pray, offer the result to Waheguru.
Udam, effort, striving. Trust and effort together: udam with one hand, bhaana with the other. Act, and leave the rest.
Your line: act, then release. One hand works and one hand opens, like the farmer's. That's day four hundred eighty-one.

482.title: Ashtpadi 12, salok: the humble
482.howItsDone: In a gurdwara everyone sits on the floor at the same height, with only the Guru Granth Sahib raised, and in the langar people eat side by side in rows; Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib reach this salok at the opening of the twelfth ashtpadi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, udam: one hand works, one hand opens. Your line was act, then release. Today Sukhmani opens its twelfth ashtpadi.

Shoes come off at the door of a gurdwara. Heads are covered. And if you stay, you sit on the floor. No pews, no front-row chairs, no reserved seats for donors. A surgeon sits beside a taxi driver; a grandmother beside a teenager who came straight from practice. One thing in the room is raised: the Guru Granth Sahib, on its platform under a canopy. Everyone else is at the same height, and it's low. That floor is a lesson before anyone says a word. Today the salok of the twelfth ashtpadi says it out loud.
screen: `SHOES OFF, HEAD COVERED.` → `EVERYONE SITS ON THE FLOOR.` → `ONLY THE GURU IS RAISED.`

segments.voice: The salok's two lines lean against each other. The first, in Guru Arjan's words: sukhee basai maskeeneeaa, aap nivaar tale. The meek one dwells in peace, having set the self down low. The second is the mirror: the great, great proud ones, Nanak, are worn away by their own pride. The Punjabi word for humility is nimrataa, and the salok's maskeen is its close cousin: the meek one, who claims nothing. Notice the verb, nivaar: to push aside, to remove. Humility here isn't feeling worthless. It's an action. You take the loud, insisting self and set it down, like a heavy bag at the door. The result is sukh, ease, the same sukh in Sukhmani's own name, so this salok sits close to the heart of the hymn. Why would lowering yourself bring ease? Look at what pride costs. It needs defending. It has to win the argument, get the credit, be seen at the right height. The proud person is always on guard duty; the humble one has put the guard down. Nobody can knock you off a seat you never climbed onto. The gurdwara floor, and the langar rows where people eat side by side, can be read as this salok made physical. Nobody earns a higher place there. And the salok puts the peace exactly there: in the sitting down.

segments.voice: If you can, sit on the floor for these two minutes; if not, lower your shoulders and let your chin drop a little. Picture the self as a bag you've been carrying, your reputation, your need to be right, and set it down beside you; you can pick it up later. For now, just sit low and notice whether anything gets easier.
Nimrataa. Humility: not thinking less of yourself, but setting the self down, low, the way the salok's meek one does. The salok promises that person peace.
Your line: the humble rest easy. The guard can go off duty now, and the floor holds you. Until tomorrow.

483.title: The proud fall
483.hook: the one who is proud of power will fall (Sukhmani 12)
483.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib move through the stanzas of the twelfth ashtpadi, which name pride of power, beauty, wealth and good deeds, and Sikh teaching on seva prizes service done without show.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nimrataa, humility: set the self down, and the humble rest easy. Today the twelfth ashtpadi shows the other side of the coin.

Guru Arjan makes a list in the first stanza of the twelfth ashtpadi, and it reads like a lineup of the people the world envies. The one with power. The one who is young and good-looking. The one with money and land. You'd expect a hymn about pride to stop there. It doesn't. Slipped into the same list, right beside the rich and the beautiful, is someone who seems to belong on the other team entirely: the person who is proud of being good.
screen: `POWER. YOUTH. MONEY AND LAND.` → `AND ONE MORE NAME ON THE LIST.` → `THE ONE PROUD OF BEING GOOD.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's salok said the proud are worn away by their own pride. Now the stanza shows what that pride looks like, one kind per line, each with a blunt picture of where it ends. Whoever carries the pride of ruling, the text says, sinks as low as a dog. Whoever thinks, I am young and beautiful, ends up a worm in filth. The images are harsh on purpose; Guru Arjan isn't polite about something he thinks is dangerous. Then the turn, before the stanza even reaches wealth: whoever calls himself a doer of good deeds wanders through birth after birth. Only then comes wealth: whoever is proud of money and land, he calls a blind, ignorant fool. The good-deeds line is the one that stops a reader. The Guru Granth Sahib praises good deeds, and Sikh life is full of them: serving in the langar, giving to people in need, standing up for the weak. So what's wrong with doing good? Nothing. The warning is about the calling yourself. Good done and then worn like a medal becomes the same as the crown and the bank account: something to stand on, something to be seen with. The salok's word for the proud was ahankaaree, from ahankaar, ego, the voice that says: I did this. The pride is the same in all four, and so is the fall. Pride needs height, and height means a drop. The bigger the pedestal, the farther down the floor.
screen: `POWER AND YOUTH: EACH FALLS.` · `BLUNT PICTURES, ON PURPOSE.` · `EVEN PRIDE IN GOOD DEEDS.` · `AHANKAAR: THE VOICE THAT SAYS I.` · then, large: `PRIDE FALLS.`

segments.voice: Sit quietly and let the mind run until it brings up something like, I handled that well, or I'm not like those people, or at least I'm the one who helps. When it does, don't scold it; notice it the way you'd notice a car going by, name it softly, pride, and let it pass. Even catching one is the practice.
Ahankaar, pride, ego. Pride of power, of youth, of wealth, and even of good deeds: the voice that says I did this, and every pedestal has a drop.
Your line: pride falls. Good done quietly needs no pedestal. Day four hundred eighty-three counts.
